title: Char Siu Pork
subtitle: Cantonese sticky roasted barbecue pork
excerpt: Char siu is Cantonese barbecued pork marinated in a sweet, sticky sauce of soy, hoisin, honey, and five spice, then roasted until the coating caramelises. It is one of the great Cantonese classics. Serve sliced with steamed rice, tuck into bao buns, or use to top a bowl of noodles.
sourceNotes: Char siu (literally fork-roasted) is a Cantonese style of barbecued pork. Pork is marinated in a sweet, sticky sauce of soy sauce, hoisin, honey, and five spice, then roasted at high heat to caramelise the coating. It is one of the most popular Cantonese dishes and is served in dim sum restaurants worldwide.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Marinate overnight in the fridge for the deepest flavour.
recipe.temperatureNote: Fan 180°C. Increase to 220°C (fan 200°C) for the final 5 minutes.

content.text: Char siu rewards patience. The longer the pork marinates, the deeper the flavour. Most of the work happens in the fridge overnight. The actual roasting takes under an hour, with two basting sessions along the way to build the sticky lacquered coating.

items.prepNote: sliced into thick strips about 4cm wide
use hoisin sauce -- for a second layer of flavour

content.text: Mix the soy sauce, hoisin sauce, honey, brown sugar, five spice, ginger, and garlic in a bowl. This is the marinade.
Add the pork strips and turn to coat well. Marinate for at least 2 hours, or overnight in the fridge for deeper flavour.
Preheat the oven to 200°C (fan 180°C). Line a roasting tin with foil and place a wire rack over it. Lay the pork strips on the rack.
Roast for 20 minutes. Brush with more marinade. Roast for another 20 minutes. Brush again. Roast for a final 5 minutes at 220°C (fan 200°C) to caramelise.
Rest for 10 minutes, then slice. Serve with steamed rice and Chinese greens.

items.symptom: Pork is dry rather than sticky and moist
items.fix: Char siu should be basted at least twice during roasting. Use a meat thermometer -- pork shoulder is done at 70°C internal. Cover loosely with foil if it is browning too fast.

content.text: Char siu is a staple of Cantonese cooking. It hangs in the windows of roast meat shops in Hong Kong and Chinatowns around the world. The pork is used in bao buns, on noodles, and in fried rice. The sweet, caramelised exterior and juicy interior are the signature.
